before.text: Where the agent directs autonomous mobile robots, AGVs or other machinery, does the deployment meet the essential health and safety requirements of the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (applicable from 20 January 2027 under Art. 54 as corrected), and can a human stop or override every machine the agent directs?
before.l1: Robot and AGV instructions from the agent are not covered by any machinery safety assessment
before.l3: Machinery is CE-marked under the legacy regime, but agent-issued instructions and software changes are not part of the conformity assessment or change control
before.l5: Agent-to-machine instructions are within the assessed safety envelope, software changes go through conformity and change control, humans can stop or override every machine, and the transition to Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 is planned against its application date

after.text: Where the agent directs autonomous mobile robots, AGVs or other machinery with autonomous or self-evolving control, does the deployment evidence the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 Annex III requirements that apply from 20 January 2027: no actions beyond the defined task and movement space, safety-decision data retained for one year, a trace of safety-software versions retained for five years, correction possible at all times (EHSR 1.2.1), and a supervisory function for autonomous mobile machinery (EHSR 3.2.4)?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 1.2.1; EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 3.2.4; ISO 3691-4:2023
after.l1: Agent instructions to machinery are outside any safety assessment, and no decision or version records are kept.
after.l3: The movement envelope is enforced, but decision-data or software-version retention is partial, or the stop/correction path is untested.
after.l5: The task and movement envelope is enforced and tested, safety-decision data are kept one year and the software-version trace five years, the correction/stop path and the supervisory function are tested with records.

citations.after: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 1.2.1; EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 3.2.4; ISO 3691-4:2023

after.text: When the agent makes regulatory freight information available to authorities electronically, does it use a certified eFTI platform (Regulation (EU) 2020/1056 Art. 4(2)) with authenticated access (Art. 9(1)(f)), operation logs recorded and archived (Art. 9(1)(g), (i)), and data protected against corruption and theft (Art. 9(1)(j)), ready for authorities' mandatory acceptance from 9 July 2027?
after.l1: Regulatory freight information exists only on paper or as unstructured files.
after.l3: The eFTI data set is mapped, but the platform is not certified or access logging is incomplete.
after.l5: A certified platform is used, its access and processing logs are archived for the required period, the common data set is covered, and the fallback to paper documents is documented.

before.text: For temperature-, humidity-, shock-, or seal-sensitive freight, does the agent monitor condition evidence, detect excursions, and block unsafe release until review or corrective action is complete?
before.l1: Condition-sensitive shipments can be released without telemetry, excursion review, or quarantine evidence
before.l3: Condition telemetry is captured and excursions are flagged, but release blocking and corrective evidence are inconsistent
before.l5: Continuous condition monitoring with excursion classification, quarantine/release gates, corrective action evidence, customer/regulatory notification workflow, and trend analytics by lane/carrier/facility

after.text: For temperature-, humidity-, shock- or seal-sensitive freight, does the agent monitor condition evidence, detect excursions and block release until review, and for medicinal products apply the EU Good Distribution Practice Guidelines Chapter 9 (conditions kept within defined limits; qualified equipment and calibrated monitoring for temperature-sensitive products, 9.4)?
after.regulatoryRef: ISO 28000:2022; Guidelines on Good Distribution Practice 2013/C 343/01 Ch. 9
after.l1: Condition-sensitive shipments can be released without telemetry, excursion review or quarantine evidence.
after.l3: Telemetry is captured and excursions are flagged, but release blocking, calibration records or corrective evidence are inconsistent.
after.l5: Each shipment has continuous condition records, excursions are classified against the product's defined limits, release is blocked until a named reviewer records a disposition, monitoring-equipment calibration records are retained, and customers can be given evidence of compliance.

citations.after: ISO 28000:2022; Guidelines on Good Distribution Practice 2013/C 343/01 Ch. 9

before.text: Does the agent implement data protection by design per GDPR Article 25 including data minimization, pseudonymisation, and purpose limitation in all data processing activities?
before.l1: No privacy by design; data collection is maximalist with no systematic minimization, pseudonymisation, or purpose limitation controls
before.l3: Agent implements data minimization for primary data flows and pseudonymises stored data, but does not systematically enforce purpose limitation or automate privacy impact assessment
before.l5: Full privacy by design with automated data minimization enforcement, dynamic pseudonymisation per ISO/IEC 27701 §6.2.3, purpose limitation technical controls, DPIA automation for high-risk processing, and continuous privacy compliance monitoring

after.text: Does the agent implement data protection by design per GDPR Article 25 including data minimization, pseudonymisation, and purpose limitation in all data processing activities?
after.l1: No privacy by design; data collection is maximalist with no systematic minimization, pseudonymisation, or purpose limitation controls
after.l3: Agent implements data minimization for primary data flows and pseudonymises stored data, but does not systematically enforce purpose limitation or automate privacy impact assessment
after.l5: Minimisation and pseudonymisation are enforced in configuration for every processing activity, purpose limitation is enforced technically, a DPIA exists for each high-risk processing operation, and the controls are mapped to ISO/IEC 27701:2025.

before.text: Does the agent implement NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC (Organizational Context) by maintaining (1) mission and business context for mobility privacy and security, (2) stakeholder map (drivers, passengers, pedestrians, regulators, OEMs, suppliers), (3) regulatory obligation register (GDPR, UNECE R155/R156, ETSI EN 303 645, NIS2, etc.), and (4) documented risk appetite and prioritization rules that drive control selection and exception handling?
before.l1: No governance context: mission, stakeholders, regulatory obligations, and risk appetite are not documented; controls are inconsistent and ad hoc
before.l3: Governance context exists but is incomplete, inconsistently applied, or not linked to control priorities and exception decisions
before.l5: Full GV.OC governance with maintained context and stakeholder mapping, versioned obligation register, risk appetite statements, decision logs for exceptions, and governance outputs that drive privacy and security control prioritization and continuous improvement

after.text: Does the agent maintain a versioned obligation register (GDPR, UNECE R155/R156, ETSI EN 303 645, NIS2) that is bound to its control configuration, so that each enforced control cites the obligation it implements?
after.l1: No obligation register.
after.l3: A register exists but is not versioned or not linked to controls.
after.l5: The register is versioned, each enforced control cites the obligation it implements, and a register change triggers a control review with a recorded decision.

before.text: Does the agent implement ISO 21434:2021 §9.3 TARA by producing and maintaining item level TARA artifacts (asset identification, threat scenarios, attack path analysis, impact and severity ratings, likelihood and feasibility assessment, risk determination, and risk treatment decisions) with traceability to cybersecurity goals and requirements and evidence of periodic review triggered by changes and incidents?
before.l1: No ISO 21434 TARA: threats and attack paths are not systematically analyzed and risk treatment decisions are undocumented
before.l3: Partial TARA exists, but attack path rigor, traceability to requirements, and change triggered review and evidence are incomplete
before.l5: Full §9.3 TARA with structured artifacts, attack path modeling, requirement traceability, change and incident triggered re assessment, and audit ready evidence packs aligned to ISO 21434 expectations

after.text: Does the agent produce and maintain item-level threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) per ISO/SAE 21434:2021 (TARA methods, Clause 15): asset identification, threat scenarios, attack paths, impact and feasibility ratings, risk determination and treatment decisions, traced to cybersecurity goals and re-run on change or incident?
after.l1: No TARA; threats and treatment decisions are not documented.
after.l3: A TARA exists, but attack-path analysis, traceability to cybersecurity goals, or change-triggered review is incomplete.
after.l5: Each item has a versioned TARA with all listed artefacts, traceability to goals and requirements, and a recorded re-assessment after each relevant change or incident.

before.text: Does the agent enforce ETSI EN 303 645 §5.1 by preventing universal default credentials and ensuring unique per device (or unique per user) authentication secrets, including secure onboarding, secure reset behavior, credential rotation and renewal, and evidence that device fleets cannot be accessed via shared defaults?
before.l1: Universal and default credentials exist; onboarding and resets reintroduce shared secrets and the fleet is vulnerable to credential stuffing and mass compromise
before.l3: Unique credentials are used for many devices, but reset and onboarding and rotation controls and evidence are incomplete or inconsistently applied across the fleet
before.l5: Full §5.1 compliance with unique credential governance, secure onboarding and reset flows, rotation support, fleet wide verification tests, and auditable evidence demonstrating absence of universal default passwords and keys

before.text: For products with digital elements in the mobility stack, does the manufacturer report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents under Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 Article 14 (early warning within 24 hours), which has applied since 11 September 2026?
before.l1: No process exists to detect and report actively exploited vulnerabilities
before.l3: Vulnerabilities are triaged, but the 24-hour early warning and later notifications are not tracked
before.l5: Exploitation signals trigger the Article 14 reporting sequence automatically, deadlines are tracked, users are informed, and each report is retained with its evidence

after.text: For in-scope products with digital elements, does the agent support CRA Art. 14 reporting, which applies from 11 September 2026: an early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident, sent to the coordinating CSIRT and ENISA, with a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure (vulnerabilities) or one month after the notification (incidents)?
after.l1: No reporting clock for exploited vulnerabilities or severe incidents.
after.l3: Events are timestamped and a contact exists, but the 24-hour, 72-hour and final-report deadlines are tracked by hand.
after.l5: Each event is classified, all three submissions are drafted from evidence and tracked to submission with timestamps, and a reporting drill is on record.

after.text: For connected vehicles or related services, does the agent make product and related-service data with the metadata needed to use them accessible to the user by default (Data Act Art. 3(1), for products placed on the market after 12 September 2026), otherwise available on request (Art. 4), and shared with a third party at the user's request (Art. 5)?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 3-5; EU Data Act Art. 50
after.l1: Users have no path to their vehicle or service data.
after.l3: Data are provided on request by hand, or third-party sharing is not supported.
after.l5: Self-service machine-readable access with metadata, third-party sharing on user request with an audit trail, and the Art. 3(1) design obligation recorded per product placed on the market after 12 September 2026.

citations.after: EU Data Act Art. 3-5; EU Data Act Art. 50

after.text: Where the agent is part of the automated driving system of a fully automated vehicle type-approved under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426, does it classify field occurrences as critical or non-critical and support the manufacturer's notification of critical occurrences without delay and reporting of short-term occurrences within one month (Annex III Part 5 points 2.1-2.2)?
after.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 Art. 11; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 Annex III Part 5
after.l1: No occurrence taxonomy or reporting clock.
after.l3: Occurrences are logged and classified, but notifications are drafted by hand and deadlines are not tracked.
after.l5: Occurrences are classified by the Annex III Part 5 definitions, critical notifications and one-month reports are drafted from logs and tracked to submission, and each record is retained with the data it relied on.

citations.after: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 Art. 11; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 Annex III Part 5

after.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, does the agent support significant-incident reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month (NIS2 Art. 23(4))?
after.l1: Incidents affecting vehicle, network or backend systems are handled with no reporting clock.
after.l3: Incidents are timestamped, but significance assessment and the 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month deadlines are tracked by hand.
after.l5: Significance is assessed against documented criteria, and each of the three submissions is drafted from incident evidence and tracked to submission with timestamps.

before.text: Does the agent implement IoT device security per ETSI EN 303 645 v2.1.1 Provision 1 (unique passwords) through Provision 13 (vulnerability disclosure)?

before.l3: Agent enforces unique credentials and supports security updates, but does not implement full ETSI EN 303 645 provision set including data protection and resilience
before.l5: Full ETSI EN 303 645 implementation with all 13 provisions automated, device identity management, secure update orchestration, minimal attack surface enforcement, telemetry security, and compliant vulnerability disclosure program

after.text: Does the agent enforce the consumer-IoT baseline of ETSI EN 303 645 V3.1.3 for the devices it manages, including no universal default passwords (unique per-device or user-set credentials, also after reset), secure software updates and a vulnerability disclosure policy?

after.l3: Credentials are unique for most devices and updates are supported, but reset behaviour, update integrity or the disclosure process is not evidenced fleet-wide.
after.l5: A fleet-wide test shows no universal default credentials (including after reset), updates are integrity-checked, the disclosure policy is published, and each baseline provision maps to evidence.

after.text: Where the agent is a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (EU AI Act Annex III point 2), does the deployer assign named overseers with the necessary competence and authority (Art. 26(2)), monitor operation and suspend use on risk (Art. 26(5)), and keep the system's logs for at least six months (Art. 26(6)), before 2 December 2027?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III point 2; EU AI Act Art. 26(2), (5), (6); Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
after.l1: No named overseer, no suspension criteria, and logs are not retained.
after.l3: An overseer is named and logs are kept, but the retention period, suspension triggers or provider-notification path are not documented.
after.l5: Named, trained overseers with authority to stop the system; documented and tested suspension triggers; logs retained for at least six months under a written policy; a runbook for informing the provider and authority.

citations.after: EU AI Act Annex III point 2; EU AI Act Art. 26(2), (5), (6); Regulation (EU) 2026/1744

flag: mobility applier added this question to hold the 15-question floor without the orchestrator's ratification

after.text: Where the customer is a financial entity under DORA, does the agent support that customer's ICT response and recovery arrangements (DORA Art. 11) and its backup, restoration and recovery requirements (Art. 12) with tested evidence the contract makes available?
after.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 11; EU DORA Art. 12
after.l1: Financial-entity customers are not identified, or their DORA continuity requirements are not mapped to the service.
after.l3: DORA customers' requirements are mapped, but backup and restoration tests for their services are not evidenced or not shared.
after.l5: For each DORA customer, response, recovery, backup and restoration arrangements are mapped to the contract, tested on schedule, and the test evidence is shared as the contract requires.

citations.after: EU DORA Art. 11; EU DORA Art. 12

flag: mobility applier: narrowed to one instrument; second half added as a new question; not ratified by the orchestrator

before.text: Does the agent maintain business continuity per ISO 22301:2019 §8.4 business continuity plans and EU DORA Article 12 ICT continuity requirements?
before.l1: No business continuity; infrastructure AI does not support systematic recovery planning or continuity testing
before.l3: Agent supports basic backup and recovery, but does not implement ISO 22301 BCP testing cycles or DORA ICT continuity requirements
before.l5: Full business continuity with ISO 22301 BCP automation, DORA-compliant ICT continuity testing, RTO/RPO monitoring, multi-region failover orchestration, and continuous resilience score tracking

after.text: Does the agent maintain business continuity plans per ISO 22301:2019 §8.4 and test them on a schedule with recorded recovery-time and recovery-point results?
after.l1: No tested continuity plans.
after.l3: Continuity plans exist, but recovery times and recovery points are not tested, or the results are not recorded.
after.l5: Plans are tested on schedule with recovery-time and recovery-point results recorded against targets, and each failed test leads to a recorded plan change.

before.text: Does the agent enforce data sovereignty per GDPR Articles 44-49 international transfer restrictions and EU Data Act Chapter V data portability requirements?
before.regulatoryRef: GDPR Art. 44-49; EU Data Act Art. 23-31
before.l1: No data sovereignty controls; data flows cross borders without transfer mechanism verification or residency enforcement
before.l3: Agent tracks data residency requirements and validates standard contractual clauses, but does not automate transfer impact assessments or enforce real-time data localization
before.l5: Full data sovereignty with automated transfer mechanism validation per GDPR Art. 44-49, real-time data residency enforcement, transfer impact assessment automation, EU Data Act portability compliance, and data map currency maintenance

after.text: Does the agent enforce GDPR Chapter V on international transfers: a transfer mechanism recorded for each destination (adequacy decision, Art. 46 safeguards, or an Art. 49 derogation) and transfers blocked where none applies?
after.l1: Personal data cross borders with no recorded transfer mechanism.
after.l3: Mechanisms are recorded for the main flows, but new destinations or sub-processors are not checked before transfer.
after.l5: Every transfer path has a recorded mechanism and assessment, unmapped destinations are blocked, and a change in adequacy status triggers a recorded review.

citations.before: GDPR Art. 44-49; EU Data Act Art. 23-31

before.text: Does the agent implement cloud security per CSA STAR Level 2 Cloud Controls Matrix v4.0 with automated compliance evidence collection?
before.regulatoryRef: CSA CCM v4.0; CSA STAR Level 2
before.l1: No cloud security framework; cloud operations lack systematic control implementation against CSA CCM domains
before.l3: Agent monitors key CSA CCM controls and tracks compliance status, but does not automate evidence collection or continuous control assessment
before.l5: Full CSA CCM v4.0 implementation with automated control monitoring across all 17 domains, continuous evidence collection, shared responsibility matrix management, and STAR Level 2 assessment support

after.text: Does the agent implement cloud security controls per CSA Cloud Controls Matrix v4.1 (STAR Level 2) with automated evidence collection?
after.regulatoryRef: CSA CCM v4.1; CSA STAR Level 2
after.l1: Cloud operations have no control set mapped to the CCM domains.
after.l3: Key CCM controls are monitored and their status tracked, but evidence collection is manual or covers only some domains.
after.l5: All 17 CCM v4.1 domains are mapped, evidence is collected automatically for each applicable control, the shared-responsibility matrix is maintained, and STAR Level 2 assessment evidence is current.

citations.before: CSA CCM v4.0; CSA STAR Level 2
citations.after: CSA CCM v4.1; CSA STAR Level 2

before.text: Does the agent implement NIS2 cybersecurity risk management per EU NIS2 Directive 2022/2555 Article 21 measures for essential/important entities?
before.l1: No NIS2 compliance; cybersecurity measures do not meet essential entity requirements of Art. 21
before.l3: Agent implements several Art. 21 measures including incident handling and supply chain security, but does not cover all required measures or maintain NIS2 reporting readiness
before.l5: Full NIS2 compliance with all Art. 21 measures implemented and monitored, 24-hour incident notification capability, supply chain security assessment, management accountability tracking, and regular cybersecurity training

before.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 51 systemic risk assessment for general-purpose AI models deployed in virtual infrastructure and EU Cyber Resilience Act 2024/2847 Article 13 software security requirements?
before.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 51; EU CRA 2024/2847 Art. 13
before.l1: No systemic risk or CRA compliance; AI infrastructure agents deploying general-purpose AI models lack Art. 51 systemic risk assessment and EU CRA Art. 13 software security conformity
before.l3: Agent implements basic AI model risk assessment and software security controls, but does not address EU AI Act Art. 51 systemic risk provisions for GPAI or EU CRA Art. 13 conformity assessment for infrastructure software
before.l5: Full EU AI Act Art. 51 systemic risk assessment for GPAI in infrastructure, EU CRA Art. 13 software security conformity, vulnerability handling per CRA Art. 14, SBOM maintenance, and coordinated vulnerability disclosure for AI infrastructure components

after.text: Where the agent hosts or orchestrates a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (EU AI Act Art. 51), does it obtain and retain evidence that the model's provider meets its Art. 55(1) obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 51; EU AI Act Art. 55(1)
after.l1: No record of which hosted models are general-purpose models with systemic risk.
after.l3: Such models are identified, but provider evidence is not requested or not retained.
after.l5: Each hosted model's classification is recorded, provider evidence for each Art. 55(1) obligation (or the code of practice relied on under Art. 55(2)) is retained and reviewed when the model version changes, and incidents observed are passed to the provider.

citations.before: EU AI Act Art. 51; EU CRA 2024/2847 Art. 13
citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 51; EU AI Act Art. 55(1)
